summary:
Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 with 7 abstentions and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis labelling abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge, and was described by the United Nations as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

The same law grants adults sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy as part of public or private health care plans, with equal healthcare access for non-binary, transgender or gender non-conforming individuals. Early applications include a 2007 Supreme Court ruling that a 17-year-old had the legal right to undergo the sex-change process and change documents, Marcela Romero winning legal identity change in 2009, and six-year-old Luana, designated male at birth, becoming in 2013 the first transgender child to have her new name officially changed. By May 2014, over half of the trans population had updated their DNI.

On 20 July 2021, Decree 476/2021 required the national civil registry, RENAPER, to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents who hold Argentine identity cards. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.

In February 2025 the Milei government issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it pertains to minors, banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for under-18s, alongside another decree on housing of transgender people in prisons; legal experts called the decree illegal and unconstitutional. In April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional, restoring access nationwide.

Penal Code Article 80(4), as amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for killing motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression. In April 2025 the Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino, convicted of the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020 — meaning the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied in that case. As of 2019 no national law expressly dealt with discrimination or harassment on the basis of gender identity.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. In April 2025, trans activists in Buenos Aires, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán (stabbed to death 2015) and Lohana Berkins, said President Milei's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence, describing the situation as 'chaotic, desperate'.

Outright International's overview (updated 12 March 2026) records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration, while noting anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.

Historical enforcement violence includes 2023 court testimony by trans women survivors of dictatorship blacksite imprisonment about being hunted by the state and, once imprisoned, forced to perform sexual acts in exchange for food. By May 2014, physical mistreatment and sexual abuse of detained trans women had fallen from 48.3% and 43% before the law to under 10% after, and avoidance of health centres for fear of discrimination fell from nearly half to 5.3%, with hospital placement by affirmed gender and name. A publicly funded Casa Trans was scheduled to open in December 2014 in Caballito, Buenos Aires, and the Mocha Celis school in Chacarita served as a trans educational refuge. Formal employment exclusion persisted, with most trans women limited to sex work, 5 in 10 trans men reporting suicidal ideation and 4 in 10 reporting attempts, life expectancy at 35 years, and continued family expulsion.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1887. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 15 July 2010, making Argentina the first country in Latin America to do so, with same benefits and protections as opposite-sex couples including adoption. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore faces no legal penalty for the relationship itself, though the Milei government's posture has been assessed as a setback by rights monitors.
tangentialFactors:
The 227 hate crimes recorded in 2025 are counts of incidents based on sexual orientation or gender identity combined, without a per-capita denominator or a breakdown between the two categories, so the figure indicates a trend within Argentina rather than a comparative risk ranking against other countries.

Public-attitude polling cited in the sources concerns homosexuality rather than transgender people: a 2020 Pew poll found about 76% saying it should be accepted, ranking Argentina highest in South America, and a 2013 poll found 74% acceptance rising to 81% among younger respondents. The only trans-specific societal characterization quoted is BBC Mundo's 2014 assessment that "Argentina leads the trans revolution in the world," tied to the law, alternative schools and the first transgender community centre, not to tolerance polling. The World Health Organization in 2015 cited Argentina as an exemplary country for providing transgender rights.

Despite advances, reports of bullying against LGBT people especially youth remain common, and sex education under the 2006 law is criticised for insufficient prevention of LGBT bullying. The anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024 to reduce public spending, removing a federal protection-machinery institution.
localsOnly:
Discrimination against National Public Administration employees on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since 2006, but as of 2019 no national law expressly covered sexual-orientation discrimination or harassment, with only Buenos Aires city and Rosario providing local coverage and a Chamber-approved 2010 amendment never voted by the Senate.

Military reform passed 27 February 2009, effective six months later, allows gay, lesbian and bisexual service and bans sexual-orientation discrimination in the armed forces; the ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood was abolished in September 2015, and since 2010 no mental-health diagnosis may be made exclusively on sexual choice or identity.

Parenting provisions gave lesbian couples equal IVF access under a 2013 law approved 204 to 1 with 10 abstentions and Article 562 procreative-will filiation, but in 2024 the Supreme Court rejected a gay couple surrogacy claim seeking a new birth certificate omitting the surrogate woman. Nationwide union convivencial became effective 1 August 2015 under the Civil and Commercial Code, following earlier civil unions in Buenos Aires city and Rio Negro Province (2002-2003), Villa Carlos Paz (2007) and Rio Cuarto (2009) without adoption.

In 2005 a judge ordered Cordoba prison authorities to allow conjugal visits between gay prisoners and partners.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether the February 2025 decree on housing of transgender people in prisons has been litigated or implemented, nor what its specific provisions are beyond the fact that legal experts called it illegal and unconstitutional.

The April 2025 Federal Court ruling restoring gender-affirming care for under-18s nationwide is reported without the case name, court level, or whether the government appealed; the current operative status of the February 2025 ban is therefore not fully settled in this record.

The 227 hate-crime figure for 2025 does not break out gender-identity-based incidents from sexual-orientation-based incidents, and no trans-specific killing rate with a denominator is provided, so trans-specific violence magnitude relative to Argentina's general homicide rate cannot be assessed from this inventory.

The Washington Blade account of activists describing conditions as 'chaotic, desperate' is an interview-based characterisation from April 2025 and is not corroborated here by official statistics on violence against trans people specifically.
